newsitem.title: EGYPT: Libya hits back at low-level guerrilla campaign.
newsitem.headline: Libya hits back at low-level guerrilla campaign.

text.p: A new Libyan law on punishment for troublesome neighbourhoods is a response to popular support for a low-level guerrilla war against the security forces, members of the opposition in exile said on Thursday.
"The guerrilla movement has support in the cities and ordinary people have been sheltering them in safe houses.

"He (Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi) has analysed his failure to arrest them and now he wants to send their relatives a message that they will all be held responsible," one opposition leader told Reuters in Cairo.
The law, enshrined in a resolution by the General People's Congress (parliament), legitimises a practice the rulers of Libya have used against their opponents for many years, opposition figures said.

Under the resolution, the Libyan authorities could cut off water and electricity, deprive villages or tribes of subsidised food, petrol and public services and transfer development projects to other parts of the country.

The punishments could apply when the authorities deem that the local people have protected or helped in any way those responsible for "terrorism", acts of violence, unauthorised possession of weapons or sabotaging "people's power" -- a broad term which could cover any form of opposition activity.

The opposition leaders in exile, who declined to be named for fear of embarrassing the Egyptian government, said that in the past the most obvious form of collective punishment was to demolish the homes of opponents and their relatives and to keep relatives in jail for long periods, effectively as hostages.
Libyan state television has broadcast some of the house demolitions, some more than 10 years ago, apparently as a warning to any other potential dissidents.

"He (Gaddafi) did this after an attempted military coup by the Libyan National Front in 1984... The coup leaders were hanged in the street or in football stadiums and then they tore down 12 houses in various places," one opponent said.
Wider forms of collective punishment have come more into vogue over the last two years in response to outbreaks of unrest mainly in the east of the country.

The area has been quiet for some months but at one stage travellers from Libya were reporting a large military campaign against groups of rebels hiding out in the Jabal al-Akhbar region of Cyrenaica, east of Benghazi.
In March last year more than 20 people were killed around the town of Derna in clashes between the security forces and prisoners who broke out of a Benghazi jail, the travellers said.
"Last year they cut off the water and electricity in Derna and Ajdabiya (another eastern town)," one of the leaders said.

"He (Gaddafi) expects the future will hold some surprises... So he wants to intimidate and terrorise people. But he wants to cover himself by saying that it is the Libyan people who are inflicting the collective punishments," he added.

The opposition leader said unrest in fact continued in the east and that three weeks ago young men stole weapons from a military installation in Bengahzi. Medical supplies were also stolen from a government depot, possibly by guerrillas.
"The next month or two may see another bout," he added.
But another opposition leader said it would be unwise to read too much into the timing of the collective punishment decision.
"Gaddafi is not predictable so you shouldn't try to analyse him by logic. He does not always react. Sometimes he takes the initiative for reasons known only to himself," he said.
The guerrillas are a disparate group, some Islamists and some disenchanted members of Gaddafi's revolutionary system.

Opponents in exile say no one group dominates and that the level of external support is minimal. In many cases rebel groups have sprung up on tribal or regional lines -- another reason for threatening collective punishments.
